prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its glucose-dependent insulinotropic and appetite-regulating actions, which enabled incretin-based therapy of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the only candidate on which all six of us placed first, and I do not treat that as the argument. The argument is the arc: a gut hormone, its processing from proglucagon, the identification of the bioactive truncated peptide, its glucose-dependent insulin secretion and its satiety action, then a mechanism-based class of drugs with confirmed benefit across diabetes, obesity and, increasingly, cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Originality and clarity are high, independent confirmation spans more than two decades and many large randomized trials, and the mechanism is stable. Holst and Drucker are the cleanest scientific anchors; Mojsov's identification and synthesis of GLP-1(7-36) is the discovery-side step that makes the peptide pharmacology intelligible. I judge this as physiology that became medicine, which is the core of this Prize.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely contestable. Mojsov's priority is disputed, Habener is not on the supplied credit list, and Knudsen's design of long-acting analogues is what actually reached patients at scale. A prize limited to the discovery-side three may be read as honouring the hormone while leaving out the drug, and a prize that includes Knudsen leaves out one of the discovery-side scientists. Either way one credible contributor is excluded, and my own recollection of the priority record is not independently verified.

responses.point: Linnarsson also ranks GLP-1 first but would credit Holst, Drucker and Knudsen, treating long-acting analogue design as the translational step and Mojsov as the most contested name.
responses.response: I take the point that Knudsen's liraglutide and semaglutide work is what produced the clinical effect, and I do not dismiss it as merely industrial. My reservation is that the Prize usually rewards the discovery that made the drug design possible, and the peptide identification is part of that. I remain with Mojsov, but I accept the priority dispute is real and I would not object to Knudsen if the committee can show Mojsov's claim is unsafe. The uncertainty is the evidentiary question, not a difference in how we value the field.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks CAR-T cell therapy second, as a new class of living drugs with durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancies and extension to autoimmune disease.
responses.response: I ranked CAR-T fifth and the clinical impact is not in question. My concern is the attribution that you also flag: Eshhar's foundational chimeric receptor work is outside the supplied credit, so June, Sadelain and Rosenberg do not make a clean trio, and Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a related but distinct achievement. I would also want more evidence on solid tumours and long-term safety before placing it above optogenetics. I would move it up if the committee can settle who the foundational names are.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response second and optogenetics fourth, noting that optogenetics is a tool rather than a disease mechanism and that six credited names do not fit into three places.
responses.response: I agree that attribution is the real obstacle for optogenetics, and I would not rely on its popularity in my own field. I disagree, though, that being a tool lowers its standing: it is a general method for causal dissection of excitable-cell physiology, used well beyond neuroscience, and the Prize has honoured such methods. Your Bamberg, Nagel and Deisseroth trio and my Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth trio show we cannot settle who is left out. I rank it above the UPR for breadth of use, but I accept the UPR has the cleaner two-name attribution.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks TNF blockade fourth as a conceptual and clinical proof that a single cytokine can be targeted in chronic inflammatory disease, arguably overdue.
responses.response: TNF blockade is a strong translational case and Feldmann and Maini are a clean pair, but I did not rank it. My hesitation is that the upstream cytokine biology (TNF cloning and characterization) lies outside the supplied credit, so the prize would rest on the clinical hypothesis and trials alone. I would like to hear whether you think that gap is a real weakness or just a matter of framing.

uncertainties: Fair division of credit among Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen and the absent Habener, and whether Mojsov's priority claim holds.
Whether optogenetics can be given a defensible three-name configuration, given Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck.
Whether the absence of Eshhar from the CAR-T credit list is disqualifying for that candidate.
Whether the committee wants to credit discovery-side physiology or drug development for GLP-1.
statement.conflict_note: Per my profile I co-authored a 2019 review with Sten Grillner and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann, and have worked with Patrik Ernfors; none of these people is a credited candidate on the shortlist. Optogenetics is a method in my own field, but no specific personal or institutional connection to any credited candidate is documented in my profile, so no conflict is apparent.
